MBC SPIKE 6-Way Expander (EXP6) × Pybricks blocks

Control EXP6 with Pybricks blocks in three steps

Blocks follow the same order as MicroPython: first import the library under "set up", then create an object and give EXP6 a name, and finally, under "program", use that name to call functions (turn motors, read sensors). Work through the steps on the left and the blocks on the right grow with you. These block pictures were built in Pybricks Code and exported as they are, so they look exactly like what you see on screen.

Check first: Pybricks block coding needs a licence code or a Patreon membership. Without one, you can write MicroPython instead; it works exactly the same way (switch the right side to "Matching MicroPython" to see it). EXP6 only works with the SPIKE Prime hub, and it needs its own battery, or the motors will not move.

1

Import the library

The first thing in a block program is a red "from … import …" block under the yellow "set up" block. It tells Pybricks to use the EXP6 library. EXP6 has only this one library, so there is nothing to choose.

  1. Download the library (save the file and keep its name): MBC_exp6_obj_Lib.py. The file name is MBC_exp6_obj_Lib.py.
  2. In Pybricks Code, click "Import a file" in the file panel on the left and import it into the same project. Do not rename the file.
  3. Click "+" to add a new file and choose to write it with blocks.
  4. Drag the red "from … import …" block out of the block list and attach it under "set up". Choose MBC_exp6_obj_Lib in the first box and MBC_EXP6 in the second.
2

Create an object: give EXP6 a name

Drag a red "… is a …" block and attach it under the import block. On the far left is the name you give EXP6; after it come the hub port and whether to use multitasking. From then on, you choose this name every time you turn a motor or read a sensor.

Which hub port is the EXP6 Host cable plugged into?

Give it a name (in Pybricks you can use any English name; here are three to try):

Do you want multitasking? (the green true / false on the block)

The port box takes the hub port: on SPIKE 1 to 6 = A to F, so 3 is port C. The first number in a function block is the expansion port on EXP6, 1 to 6. Do not mix them up.

3

Use the functions

Put a red function block under "program": choose the name exp6 in the first box, await in the middle and the function in the last box. Then click the ">" on the right to add boxes for the values (the first is usually the expansion port, 1 to 6). Click a function and the blocks and output switch to its example.

Simulated EXP6 (seen from above): choose what is plugged into each expansion port, then watch the motors turn and see what is printed on the right

At the start, expansion ports 1 and 2 have motors, port 4 a colour sensor, port 5 an ultrasonic sensor and port 6 a force sensor, the same ports the examples use. The simulation is only an illustration: 1% motor speed counts as 10 degrees per second (a real motor depends on its model), and the sensor values are simplified. The red pointer shows which way the motor shaft points; ↻ = clockwise. When you unplug the expander, the motors stop and every reading becomes 0 (not the last value). The library prints its connection warnings in both Chinese and English, so you see them here exactly as on the hub. About 0.5 seconds after the program ends, the EXP6 watchdog stops the motors (a turn that has not finished yet finishes first).

Block examples for every function

33 functions, each with a set of blocks you can copy (name exp6, multitasking true). Actions such as turning or stopping a motor usually go under "program" and run once. Readings go inside a repeat loop and are read again and again. Click "Try it" to jump to step 3; the blocks and output on the right switch to that example.

Things to know

    
    
      
  1. Import the library file into the project first. If MBC_exp6_obj_Lib.py is not imported, you cannot choose MBC_EXP6 in the red blocks.
    2. 
      
  2. await and call must match multitasking: with multitasking true choose await; with multitasking false choose call. If you mix them, the program fails on the hub.
    3. 
      
  3. Wait with the keep_alive_wait function, not a long wait block. If EXP6 hears nothing from the hub for more than 0.5 seconds, it stops the motors by itself (a watchdog). The multitasking version of the blocks uses Pybricks' own run_task, which does not send a heartbeat in the background. So when you need to wait longer than 0.5 seconds, use a function block, choose keep_alive_wait and enter the milliseconds (the 100 ms wait inside a loop is fine). After the program ends, EXP6 stops the motors within 0.5 seconds by itself. If you want them to stop the moment the program ends, write MicroPython instead and use the library's run_task.
    4. 
      
  4. Do not mix up the two kinds of port number: the "is a" block takes the hub port (1 to 6 = A to F); the first number in a function block is the expansion port on EXP6. EXP6 only accepts LEGO motors and the LEGO colour, ultrasonic and force sensors.
    5. 
      
  5. Unplugging the expander does not stop the program: readings become 0 (not the last value), the computer prints a warning at most once a second, and it reconnects by itself when you plug it back in. A turn (motor_run_degrees, motor_track_target) moves on right away and does not wait for the turn to finish, so add a keep_alive_wait after it. Blocks cannot read the connected attribute or call the object's run_task; to use them, write MicroPython instead.
    6.
